lead: Sunlight leaves the sun as broad-spectrum energy, crosses the atmosphere, strikes a surface, and travels back up to a sensor. On both trips the atmosphere scatters and absorbs part of it. At the surface the energy splits into reflected, absorbed and transmitted fractions. The sensor therefore records radiance — light arriving at the instrument — and not the reflectance of the ground. This chapter follows one beam along that path, quantifies the losses, and ends with the formula that converts measured radiance back to reflectance. Every comparison of two dates and every classification depends on that conversion.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.1 for wavelength, irradiance and radiance.

sections.h3: The path: sun, atmosphere, ground, atmosphere, sensor

blocks.text: Sunlight arrives at the top of the atmosphere as irradiance E, measured in watts per square metre (W/m²). The atmosphere removes part of it on the way down. The ground receives the rest and splits it into reflected, absorbed and transmitted fractions. On the way up the atmosphere removes more, and adds light of its own that never touched the ground. The sensor at the top records radiance L, in W m⁻² sr⁻¹ — power per unit area per unit solid angle, that is, the light arriving from one direction.

Two consequences follow. First, L is not a property of the ground alone; it depends on the sun, the atmosphere and the viewing direction. Second, a number that describes the ground must be recovered by undoing the atmospheric part. That number is reflectance.

The two trips are not equal. The downward beam is nearly parallel, so it crosses the shortest possible path. The upward beam is scattered into a wide cone and meets more air. A sensor looking straight down at noon sees the least atmosphere; a sensor looking obliquely sees much more, which is one reason off-nadir images look hazier.

sections.h3: Scattering: three regimes, set by particle size

blocks.text: Scattering redirects energy without absorbing it. The size of the particle compared with the wavelength decides the behaviour.

items: Rayleigh scattering — nitrogen and oxygen molecules, far smaller than any visible wavelength. Scattered intensity goes as 1/λ⁴. Blue light at 0.45 µm is scattered (0.70 ÷ 0.45)⁴ ≈ 5.8 times more strongly than red light at 0.70 µm. That is why the sky is blue and the direct sun looks slightly yellow, and why blue bands of satellite images are full of haze.

Mie scattering — aerosols such as dust, smoke, sea salt and pollen, roughly 0.1 µm to a few µm, close to the wavelength. It is only weakly wavelength dependent and is forward-peaked. It produces the grey-white veil over a city.
Non-selective scattering — cloud droplets and coarse dust, much larger than the wavelength. All wavelengths scatter about equally, so fog and cloud look white and hide the ground in every band.

blocks.text: Absorption converts radiation into heat. Only certain wavelengths are absorbed, because a molecule absorbs only photons whose energy matches its own transitions: water vapour near 1.4, 1.9 and 2.7 µm; carbon dioxide near 2.7 and 4.3 µm; ozone in the ultraviolet and near 9.6 µm; oxygen in narrow bands near 0.69 and 0.76 µm. Between these bands the atmosphere is largely transparent. The gaps are the atmospheric windows, and every optical sensor is built inside one.

sections.h3: Energy balance at the surface and the radiance-to-reflectance link

blocks.where: ρ is reflectance, α is absorptance and τ is transmittance — each the fraction of the energy arriving at the surface that is reflected, absorbed or passed through.

blocks.text: For an opaque surface such as soil or rock, τ = 0 and ρ + α = 1. Albedo is the reflectance averaged over the whole solar spectrum, weighted by the energy in each wavelength. Fresh snow has an albedo near 0.8–0.9 and stays cool; a dark asphalt road near 0.1 and heats up.

Reflection is specular or diffuse. A calm water surface is a mirror: almost all energy leaves at one angle equal to the incidence angle. A rough field scatters in all directions. A surface that scatters equally in every direction, so that the same radiance is seen from any viewpoint, is called Lambertian. Most natural land surfaces are approximately Lambertian.

blocks.where: ρ is reflectance (dimensionless); L is the radiance leaving the surface in W m⁻² sr⁻¹; E is the irradiance falling on it in W m⁻²; π ≈ 3.1416 carries the geometry, because a constant radiance integrated over a hemisphere gives π L.

blocks.text: Path radiance. The sensor also receives light scattered into its line of sight that never reached the ground. Call it L_p; the measured radiance is L_target + L_p. A hazy image therefore looks brighter and flatter, and a reflectance computed from it without correction is too high. Removing L_p is atmospheric correction, handled in Chapter 6.7.

figure.caption: Energy is attenuated on the way down, reflected by the ground, attenuated again on the way up, and the atmosphere adds its own light before the sensor. The sensor records radiance, so reflectance must be recovered by calculation.

spec.title: Energy path from sun to sensor
spec.aria: A vertical flow from the sun through the atmosphere to the ground, back up through the atmosphere and into the sensor, with irradiance entering and radiance leaving.

examples.question: A flat, uniform field is imaged from directly above on a clear day. The irradiance reaching the field is E = 500 W/m² and the sensor measures a radiance L = 25 W m⁻² sr⁻¹ from it. (a) Treating the field as Lambertian, find its reflectance. (b) The same field is imaged again when haze cuts the irradiance at the surface to 250 W/m², and the measured radiance falls to 12.5 W m⁻² sr⁻¹. Find the reflectance again and comment. Take π = 3.1416.
steps: Write the working formula for a Lambertian surface: ρ = π L / E.
Numerator: 3.1416 × 25 = 78.54, in W m⁻² sr⁻¹, since π is dimensionless.
So ρ = 0.157, that is 15.7 per cent reflected. The remaining 84.3 per cent is absorbed or transmitted by the soil.
Both L and E halved, so the ratio is unchanged. The radiance fell because the illumination fell, not because the field changed.
examples.answer: The field's reflectance is 0.157, or 15.7 per cent, in both cases; the radiance halved only because the irradiance halved.
examples.check:
import math

rho1 = math.pi * 25 / 500.0
print(round(rho1, 3))
print(round(rho1 * 100, 1))

rho2 = math.pi * 12.5 / 250.0
print(round(rho2, 3))

traps: Radiance is not reflectance. Radiance changes with sun angle, haze and season; reflectance does not. Convert digital numbers to reflectance before comparing two dates.
Rayleigh scattering goes as 1/λ⁴, not 1/λ, and short wavelengths scatter most. The sky is blue because blue is scattered out of the beam, not because blue is absorbed.
Albedo is a broadband average, never the reflectance of a single band. Quoting a one-band value as albedo loses marks.
Path radiance always adds to the signal. An uncorrected hazy image gives a reflectance that is too high, never too low.
For an opaque surface τ = 0, so ρ + α = 1. Writing ρ + α + τ = 1 and then setting τ = 1 reverses the physics.

quiz.q: Define irradiance and radiance, with SI units.
quiz.a: Irradiance E is power falling on unit area of a surface, in W/m². Radiance L is power per unit area per unit solid angle, in W m⁻² sr⁻¹, arriving from or leaving in one direction.

quiz.q: Name the three scattering regimes and the particle size that causes each.
quiz.a: Rayleigh — molecules much smaller than the wavelength; Mie — aerosols of size close to the wavelength; non-selective — particles much larger than the wavelength, such as cloud droplets and coarse dust.

quiz.q: Why is the sky blue, and why does the setting sun look red?
quiz.a: Rayleigh scattering varies as 1/λ⁴, so short wavelengths are scattered most and the scattered skylight reaching the eye is blue. At sunset the direct beam crosses a long air path; blue is scattered out of the line of sight and mostly long wavelengths survive, so the sun looks red.

quiz.q: Why is there no operational sensor band centred on 1.4 µm?
quiz.a: Water vapour absorbs strongly there, so very little energy reaches the ground and returns. The small, variable signal cannot give a reliable measurement of the surface.

quiz.q: A Lambertian field has reflectance ρ = 0.25 and receives irradiance E = 640 W/m². Find the radiance the sensor records. Take π = 3.1416.
A surface absorbs 0.60 of the energy arriving on it and transmits 0.05. Find its reflectance and say whether it is opaque.
quiz.a: ρ = 1 − 0.60 − 0.05 = 0.35. Since τ = 0.05 is not zero, the surface is slightly translucent, not opaque.

quiz.q: Two images of the same field, a month apart, give clearly different digital numbers. List three causes that are not a change on the ground, and the processing step that removes them.
quiz.a: Sun elevation and azimuth, atmospheric haze and path radiance, and sensor gain or calibration. Convert digital numbers to surface reflectance with atmospheric correction and illumination normalisation before comparing.

quiz.q: A calm lake appears almost black in a nadir image but blindingly bright in one off-nadir frame. Explain the difference.
quiz.a: Calm water is a specular reflector. Looking straight down, the sun's mirror image leaves away from the sensor, so only weak scattered light is recorded and the lake looks dark. At the specular angle the sun's reflection enters the sensor directly and the lake looks bright. The surface did not change; the viewing geometry did.

beyond: Not for the exam. Operational processors use radiative transfer codes such as 6S and MODTRAN to predict transmission and path radiance for a given sun angle, view angle and visibility, then invert them band by band. Space agencies publish per-band coefficients with each product so users can reach surface reflectance without running the code. Newer work couples atmosphere and surface in a single inversion, and machine learning now estimates aerosol loading directly from the image. Search for atmospheric correction, 6S radiative transfer and surface reflectance product.
